concept.body: Side-Splitter: when a line is PARALLEL to one side of a triangle, it divides the other two sides proportionally. Two equivalent forms: piece-to-piece AD/DB = AE/EC, or piece-to-whole AD/AB = AE/AC. Keep BOTH ratios in the same style; don't mix piece-to-piece with piece-to-whole.

explanationVariants: AD/DB pairs with AE/EC — piece-to-piece on both sides.
Keep the same style: piece-to-piece with piece-to-piece.

widget.prompt: To match AD/DB in a side-splitter proportion, the other ratio should be…

options.label: AE/EC
options.feedback: Piece-to-piece pairs with piece-to-piece: AD/DB = AE/EC.

options.label: AE/AC
options.feedback: That's piece-to-WHOLE — mixing styles. Match AD/DB with AE/EC.

options.label: AC/EC
options.feedback: That flips and mixes. AD/DB pairs with AE/EC.

options.label: DB/AD
options.feedback: That just inverts the first ratio. Use AE/EC to match AD/DB.

steps.body: Draw a line **parallel to one side** of a triangle, crossing the other two. The **Side-Splitter Theorem** says it cuts those two sides in the **same ratio**: AD/DB = AE/EC. It follows straight from AA similarity — the parallel line makes the small top triangle similar to the whole, so the pieces stay proportional.

predict.prompt: A line parallel to the base cuts the other two sides. Slide it up and down: can the two ratios AD/DB and AE/EC ever come apart?

options.label: Never — wherever the parallel cut sits, the two ratios stay equal
Sometimes — they only match when the cut is at the midpoint
It depends on the triangle — they match only in isosceles ones

predict.reveal: Never. Drag the cut anywhere along the sides and the two readouts move together, digit for digit — that is the side-splitter theorem, and the reason it can be used to solve for a missing length.

widget.prompt: Slide the parallel cut until AD = 4 and DB = 6 — four tenths of the way down — then read what the other side is forced to do.
widget.successFeedback: Both readouts show 0.67. That is AD/DB = 4/6 — and it is equally AE/EC = 6/9, which is why EC must be 9. Slide the cut anywhere else and the two numbers change together and stay equal: the ratio is forced, never coincidental.
widget.lowFeedback: The cut is too high — AD/DB is still under 4/6. Keep sliding down, and watch the second ratio follow the first the whole way.
widget.highFeedback: Past it — AD/DB has gone above 4/6. Ease back up. Notice that overshooting moved BOTH ratios, never just one.

explanationVariants: The parallel line creates equal corresponding angles, so the small triangle is similar to the whole (AA) — and similar triangles have proportional sides.
DE ∥ BC ⇒ △ADE ~ △ABC by AA, which forces the sides (and their pieces) into proportion.

widget.prompt: Why does a line parallel to one side split the other two proportionally?

options.label: It creates a smaller similar triangle (AA), and similar triangles have proportional sides
options.feedback: The parallel line gives equal corresponding angles, so △ADE ~ △ABC — proportional sides split each side in the same ratio.

options.label: Because parallel lines are always equal in length
options.feedback: Parallel lines aren't equal in length — the proportionality comes from the SIMILAR triangles the parallel creates.

options.label: Because the triangle is isosceles
options.feedback: There is no isosceles assumption — the theorem holds for ANY triangle, via the similar triangles.

options.label: Because the line bisects both sides
options.feedback: It bisects only in the special midsegment case. In general it splits PROPORTIONALLY, not equally.

steps.body: There's a whole-side version too: **AD/AB = AE/AC**, comparing each top piece to the FULL side. Both forms come from the same similar triangles — use whichever matches the lengths you're given. Piece-to-piece (AD/DB) or piece-to-whole (AD/AB), just keep both ratios in the same style.

widget.prompt: Using AD/AB = AE/AC: AD = 4, AB = 10, and AE = 6. Find AC.

explanationVariants: Mixing forms is the trap: AD/DB (piece-to-piece) must pair with AE/EC, and AD/AB (piece-to-whole) with AE/AC. Keep both sides in the same style.
Match the ratio style on both sides — piece-to-piece with piece-to-piece, or whole with whole.

widget.prompt: If you write AD/DB on one side, what must you write on the other for the side-splitter proportion?

options.label: AE/EC (piece-to-piece, matching the style)
options.feedback: Piece-to-piece pairs with piece-to-piece: AD/DB = AE/EC. Keep both ratios the same style.

options.label: AE/AC (piece-to-whole)
options.feedback: Mixing styles gives a wrong equation. AD/DB (piece-to-piece) must pair with AE/EC, not AE/AC.

options.label: AC/AE (whole-to-piece, flipped)
options.feedback: That both flips and mixes styles. To match AD/DB, use AE/EC.

options.label: DB/EC (both denominators)
options.feedback: That isn't a valid ratio pairing. AD/DB pairs with AE/EC.

steps.body: The **midsegment** you met earlier is just the side-splitter's most famous special case: the parallel line hits the MIDPOINTS, so the ratio is 1 : 1 and each piece is half. Every midsegment is a side-splitter; not every side-splitter is a midsegment.

widget.prompt: The midsegment (joining two midpoints) splits the sides in what ratio?

options.label: 1 : 1 — it hits the midpoints, so each piece is equal
options.feedback: Midpoints split each side into two equal pieces — the side-splitter ratio is 1 : 1.
2:1 is the centroid's median split, not the midsegment. Midpoints give 1 : 1.
A midpoint divides a side into two EQUAL halves, so 1 : 1 — not 1 : 2.

options.label: it depends on the triangle
options.feedback: It's always 1 : 1 for a midsegment, in every triangle — that's what 'midpoint' guarantees.

hints: Set up the side-splitter proportion with the algebraic pieces.
AD = x, DB = x + 2, AE = 6, EC = 9 — write x/(x+2) = 6/9.
explanationVariants: The proportion x/(x+2) = 2/3 gives 3x = 2x + 4, so x = 4.

widget.prompt: A parallel line splits the sides: AD = x, DB = x + 2, AE = 6, EC = 9. Solve for x.

commonErrors.feedback: 6 copies AE — but you must solve the proportion x/(x+2) = 6/9. That gives 3x = 2x + 4, so x = 4.

takeaways: Side-Splitter: a line ∥ one side cuts the others in equal ratios (AD/DB = AE/EC).
It works because the parallel creates a similar triangle (AA).
Match ratio styles; the midsegment is the 1 : 1 special case.
